docs.title: Four Environments: An Interactive Spatial Audio Composition
Four Environments: An Interactive Spatial Audio Composition
docs.text:
COURSE PROJECT · SPATIAL AUDIO · INTERACTIVE COMPOSITION · 2026

This project treats spatial audio as a performable instrument rather than a fixed playback format. Four environmental scenes—Water, Valley, City, and Hall—can be selected in real time while a performer reshapes their density, movement, direction, and depth with a MIDI controller. Each scene combines environmental recordings, localized sound objects, and a pitched drone layer into a continuously evolving spatial composition.

The REAPER session organizes four sound environments as independent scenes inside a shared 16-channel Ambisonics workflow.

docs.title: Water
docs.text: Muffled, diffuse, and enveloping. A wide underwater pad surrounds localized whale calls, with softened high frequencies and a slowly changing spatial field.

docs.title: Valley
docs.text: Open, deep, and distant. Longer reverberation and discrete delays suggest reflections returning from far surfaces.

docs.title: City
docs.text: Dense, lateral, and hard-edged. Short reflections and moving point sources evoke traffic, signals, and an active urban sound field.

docs.title: Hall
docs.text: Direct, warm, and controlled. Early reflections and concert-hall reverberation keep musical material present while extending it into the room.

docs.title: Performance-driven signal architecture
docs.text:
Each scene contains four sound objects with complementary spatial roles: a continuous ambience, one or two localized sources, and an object that emphasizes motion or depth. An Akai MPK Mini MK2 provides a consistent performance vocabulary across the complete work. Four pads select scenes; shared knobs control the position of equivalent sound types; additional controls shape EQ, chorus, and scene volume.

MIDI performancescene selection · position · effects → Sound objectsambience · point sources · drones → Scene busreverb · EQ · delay → 3rd-order HOA16-channel AMIX bus → Dual decodeheadphones · loudspeaker array

The production system is built in REAPER with the IEM Plug-in Suite. StereoEncoder places and widens objects; FdnReverb establishes the acoustic character of each scene; MultiEQ shapes its spectral identity; and DualDelay creates discrete reflections where they matter. Every spatial track and bus remains at 16 channels through a shared third-order HOA mix. The result is decoded either binaurally for headphones or through AllRADecoder for the spatial loudspeaker system in Couch 204.

To make the system more open and extensible, the project also explores a Pure Data implementation. The prototype recreates the Water scene from the ground up: it loads the underwater ambience and whale samples, exposes azimuth and elevation controls, manages source volume, and routes a 16-channel spatial field through the IEM plug-ins using vstplugin~.

docs.title: Continuing the system
docs.text:
The REAPER version establishes the complete composition and its live MIDI workflow; the Pure Data version establishes a reusable open-source foundation. Future development can extend the remaining three scenes, add a general-purpose sampler, integrate MIDI directly, and create new relationships between musical material and spatial movement.

docs.title: SynOrbit
docs.text:
A spatial instrument for composing with time, transforming the flat sequencer timeline into rotating orbital structures that can be seen, heard, and reshaped through gesture.

SynOrbit presentation setup · GTCMT Seed Grant Presents: Prism Pt. 1

docs.title: Sequencing as an orbit
docs.text:
SynOrbit reimagines musical time as a navigable spatial structure. Notes and patterns sit on rotating rings rather than a conventional horizontal timeline: their position around an orbit determines when they sound, while the ring’s rotation makes playback visible as continuous motion.

Hand gestures let performers create, move, and reshape these sequences in real time. The instrument turns rhythmic organization into a physical activity—something that can be reached into, reorganized, layered, and shared during improvisation.

PLACEMusical eventsnotes and patterns occupy points on a ring→ ROTATEMake time visibleorbital motion drives the playback cycle→ GESTUREReshape the sequencecreate, move, and edit events in space→ PERFORMLayered rhythmmultiple orbits form a live musical system

docs.title: The spatial interface
docs.text:
Separate orbital layers organize parallel musical patterns. Events become tangible ball-like controls distributed around each ring.

The stacked orbits provide a readable overview of several repeating patterns at once. Spatial separation distinguishes layers, rotation communicates phase, and the event objects expose the sequence as a manipulable arrangement rather than an abstract list of values.

docs.title: My contribution — Third-person perspective
docs.text:
XR03

Changda Ma’s contribution centered on the project’s third-person perspective: an external observer view for presenting an interaction that would otherwise remain largely inside the performer’s headset.

This perspective frames the performer’s actions together with the orbital sequencer and its state changes, helping collaborators and audiences understand the relationship between gesture, spatial structure, and musical time.

docs.title: Presentation and development
docs.text:
SynOrbit was presented on May 2, 2026 at Georgia Tech’s West Village 175 as part of GTCMT Seed Grant Presents: Prism Pt. 1 — Sound Through a New Lens. The ongoing project is supported by the Georgia Tech Center for Music Technology Seed Grant and continues to explore virtual instrument design, temporal interaction, gesture control, and collaborative performance.

Future iterations can extend the observer view into a more expressive performance camera, clarify visual feedback for musical state changes, and study how performers coordinate when multiple orbital timelines are active at once.
